items_missed: Identity was never confirmed. The call opened with the customer saying 'Hey, this is Dane' and Hector answering 'No, this is Hector' — a crossed introduction that was never untangled. Hector found the record ('Yup, there you are') but never said the customer's name back to verify he had the right booking, and the name is used zero times across the whole call.

No agenda statement and no confirmation ask. He went from 'I think yeah. At that rate it's probably for an auto booking' straight into the estimate breakdown. The customer had called about a voicemail from a different rep and was never told what this conversation was going to cover.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Stairs and floors never asked at either end — origin or destination. He rebuilt the estimate from scratch on this call and a stair carry is the single biggest variable on a heavy-furniture job. The customer volunteered that his couch was 'awful to move-in by myself' and that he has a lifting restriction, and Hector still never asked whether either address has stairs.

Access and parking never asked. No question about driveway, truck staging, or gate access at either address, on a house-to-house move where both addresses were already on file and could have been checked.

Box count never asked. The customer said 'the rest is just like small knick-knacks' and 'I have a truck too and I want to be loading my truck up' — meaning some unknown quantity of items is in scope and some is not, and the line between them was never drawn. That ambiguity is now sitting in a three-hour estimate.

The hourly rate was never stated. Not once. The customer's opening question was literally rate arithmetic — 'online it said that it's a two and a half hour minimum but it was for two and a half hours is it gonna be $1,400 for right down the road?' — and Hector answered with totals ($615 for the minimum, $710 for three hours) without ever saying what the per-hour, per-mover rate is. The customer still cannot check the math himself, which is what he called about.
'Pricing is super simple' opener never used.
What's-included list was partial. He covered padded blankets, shrink wrap, floor and wall protection, and tools, but never mentioned gas, truck, taxes, or insurance as included in the rate.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — a real miss with this customer, who had shoulder reconstruction a month and a half ago, cannot lift more than twenty pounds, and is relying entirely on the crew. Knowing who is walking into his house is worth more to him than to most.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

The 'no hidden fees' pitch never came, even though he spent a full minute explaining the one fee that exists. Explaining the trip fee without pairing it to 'and that's the only additional charge — no credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees' leaves the fee standing alone as a surprise rather than an exception.

Clock start never explained. He referenced the 2.5-hour minimum repeatedly and confirmed drive time is billable, but never said the clock begins on-site when the contract opens, and never mentioned fifteen-minute proration — which matters more than usual here, because the whole job is expected to land at or just past the minimum.
Walk distance never asked at either address.
No equivalents or plain-language anchor used to make three hours feel concrete.

Save Your Ass was handed to him and he only took half of it. The customer volunteered the prep himself — 'Cause I have a truck too and I want to be loading my truck up' — and Hector's whole response was 'Fantastic. Yeah, that'll definitely help out with the overall timeframe there.' Timeframe, not bill. He never connected the customer's own effort to money saved, never gave consolidation examples (the buffet, the bookshelf and the coffee table all have contents that could be emptied in advance), and never closed it with a sense-check. The customer was already doing the right thing and never got told it was worth anything.

No BOLDED-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections' ask on the confirmation email. 'I'll send you a new confirmation email just to verifying all of what we've discussed so far' gets close to the verification idea but never asks the customer to read it and reply — so the email_handoff differentiator does not count, and a re-scoped estimate that dropped from seven hours to three goes out with no explicit check that the customer agrees with the new scope.
Hours and how to reach us never given — 'just feel free to reach out' was the whole close.
Customer's name used zero times. 'Boss' was used twice instead, including in the farewell.

The no-deposit and booking-attempt bullets are auto-granted here because the job is already on the schedule, but nothing was done to deepen the commitment — no confirmation of the arrival window, no mention of what happens if he needs to reschedule.
top_strength: Hector did the single most valuable thing on this call: he found an estimate that was badly wrong and he fixed it downward, unprompted, against his own branch's revenue. The auto-booking had this job at seven hours based on square footage. The customer said 'the house is completely empty at the living room, so I'm just moving my living room furniture' and Hector immediately said 'Let me make that appropriate adjustment just so that we don't necessarily have to worry about booking a whole day and only having to worry about the living room.' He then did real inventory work to earn the new number — item by item, with the right questions: 'is there anything that has like glass incorporated, like, glass top or glass shelving glass doors,' 'for your couch, is that leather or white?', and when the customer described the buffet as marble he connected it correctly on the spot: 'Okay, gotcha, and that's why it's so heavy makes sense.' He caught the dining table risk himself and did not assume it away — 'I was actually working under the assumption that legs off' — and when the customer explained it is handmade and the legs are fixed, he re-reasoned out loud rather than silently padding. He landed at three hours and gave the total: '$710.' That is a seven-hour auto-booking corrected to three by a rep who asked better questions, and he closed it by telling the customer why it helps both of them: 'that way you know, we don't have to worry about having a crew there twiddling thumbs for the rest of the day.' His No Worries delivery was also the most operationally complete in the batch. He did not just name the $2,000 — he tied it to a specific action the customer has to take: 'we do ask with the TV that you keep the power cord with it that way we could test it before and after just make sure that it's in perfect working order so that we can include it in that no worries, damage coverage.' And when the customer asked again ('So wait real quick. What do I need to do with the TV?') he explained it a second time without a trace of impatience. He also set the TV-mount boundary clearly and early — 'The only thing that we can't do is reinstall the TV while the mount and the TV in your new home because that involves making holes and walls' — which is a move-day argument prevented on a phone call.
coaching_note: Estimate-accuracy flag, and this is the most useful thirty seconds of audio in the whole week for the bottom-4 work. Hector says the padding instinct out loud, in his own words, unprompted: 'I just have the tendency of leaning on the conservative side. You know, my experience as a mover is like, you always want to make some time for the oh, adjusting, or oh, I forgot about this, or you know complications.' He had already started padding above the minimum before the customer corrected him — he said the minimum 'might be a little optimistic' and wanted 'wiggle room' for tight corners at the destination, and only backed off when the customer told him 'It'll actually be easier to move into the newer home,' at which point Hector said 'Oh, fantastic never mind.' That is the exact mechanism behind the 47% manager-adjustment number, spoken plainly by a rep who does not realize it is a problem. Amanda: this clip is worth playing at the calibration session. The coaching is not 'stop being careful' — it is 'your wiggle room is a guess, and the customer usually has the answer, so ask instead of padding.' Hector proved that himself on this call in the space of two turns. There is also a live estimate-accuracy data point sitting in this booking that is worth pulling the actual against: an auto-booking that was set at seven hours for a whole-home square footage went out re-scoped at three hours for a living room. Both numbers came from Einstein and they are more than twice apart. When this job runs on October 7, the actual against the revised three-hour estimate is a clean test of whether re-scoping calls like this one improve accuracy — which is the argument for doing more of them. Highest-leverage coaching fix: state the rate. The customer opened the call with a rate question and closed it without ever hearing the rate. Hector gave him $615 and $710 as sealed totals, which means the customer cannot verify anything, cannot compare Einstein to another quote, and cannot check the invoice on move day. Every quote needs the rate said out loud — 'that's $205 an hour for two movers and a truck, so three hours plus the $140 trip fee comes to $710' — so the customer holds the arithmetic, not just the answer. Second: use the name. Zero uses across eleven minutes, with 'boss' twice instead. He had the record open on his screen the entire call. And because the call opened with a crossed introduction ('Hey, this is Dane' / 'No, this is Hector'), confirming the name would have done double duty as identity verification on a booking he was about to modify. Third: the filler is now load-bearing. 'Fantastic,' 'no worries,' 'cool cool,' and 'gotcha' appear so often that they stop reading as enthusiasm and start reading as a verbal tic — 'Fantastic, it's the okay, no worries' and 'Cool, awesome. Well, that's awesome' are both in here. His warmth is genuine and does not need the scaffolding. Fourth: the two missing differentiators are both free and both fit this customer specifically. He told Hector he had shoulder reconstruction six weeks ago and cannot lift twenty pounds — Meet Your Mover, one sentence, lands hard on someone who is fully dependent on the crew.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently generous and easy to talk to — real empathy on the shoulder surgery ('Understood, gotcha, gotcha, no worries'), he connected details back to what the customer said rather than just logging them ('that's why it's so heavy makes sense'), explained the TV question twice without impatience, and thanked the customer for his patience mid-estimate; held back from a 5 by never once using the customer's name and by filler so repetitive ('fantastic,' 'no worries,' 'cool cool') that it starts to flatten the warmth it is meant to carry.
audio_review_reason: The transcript has a genuine sequencing problem — the customer's 'Okay / Gotcha / Yes' turns repeatedly land before the statements they answer, so it is not possible to confirm from text whether Hector's estimate reasoning was actually delivered as a two-way conversation or as a monologue the customer acknowledged afterward. There is also an unexplained side interruption mid-call ('What's up boss? Sorry, I didn't want to interrupt you'), suggesting someone else in the room, which is worth hearing on a call where an existing booking was re-scoped and re-priced.
